lines: On a Friday, a developer retypes one column so it can finally carry a fraction, something it was never built to hold before.
The pipeline watching that table keeps running, completely unaware, and whatever sits downstream never gets told its own shape should have changed too.
From that exact moment on, every value with a fraction in it arrives, gets written, and nothing anywhere raises so much as a warning.
Think about what actually has to happen for a consumer to even notice a column is gone.
A dropped column simply stops being part of every row event from that point forward.
Does a consumer expecting that field get told it's missing somehow, or does it just quietly never arrive again?
answer: Expecting an error assumes something out there is checking for a field it can't possibly know to look for anymore.
Nothing arrives, and nothing says why, because dropping a column is handled exactly the same quiet way adding one is.

lines: Here's the one fact that explains why neither of those changes ever gets its own announcement.
I ran an actual column change against the real database and looked at exactly what came out of the decoded stream.
What came out was an opening marker and a closing one, with absolutely nothing recorded in between them at all.
I measured both halves of that same idea directly, one right after the other, on the same table.
Adding a column produced no announcement of its own; it simply showed up, for the first time, on the very next row that happened to carry it.
Dropping a column worked identically in reverse, and whatever that field held before the drop stayed frozen at the sink, with nothing ever able to touch it again.
Now here's why retyping a column isn't some separate, more dramatic kind of event.
To the stream itself, retyping produces exactly the same shape of thing adding or dropping does: one ordinary row event.
The only thing different about it is a small type label sitting next to a column name that hasn't changed at all.
I picked a genuinely demanding case to test that idea against: a value too large for the column's original type to ever hold.
The decoded stream carried the new, wider type and the full value without any trouble at all.
A sink that widened its own matching column before writing stored that exact value, with absolutely nothing lost in the process.
I reused that identical mechanism, but retyped the column toward something that could hold a fraction instead of something wider.
This time, I deliberately left the sink's own column at its original, narrower type, to see what would actually happen.
The write succeeded anyway, and the fractional part of the value was rounded away on the spot, with no error of any kind.
Not every change can be solved this cleanly, though, and it's worth naming exactly where that limit sits.
Once a column's own older rows genuinely can't be reinterpreted correctly under its new shape, no amount of widening or reapplying a type fixes that.
At that point, the only real repair left is taking a fresh, incremental snapshot of that one table.
Pull everything measured today together, and one plain rule sits underneath all of it.
Adding or dropping a column never announces itself; it only ever shows up, or stops showing up, on its own row event.
Widening survives a reader that keeps its own shape current, and narrowing punishes the reader that doesn't.
Here's a question this hasn't actually settled yet, and it matters more than it sounds.
A brand-new column shows up in a stream your own sink has genuinely never encountered before.
Something, somewhere, has to decide whether that's even allowed before a single row gets written anywhere. Whose decision is that, exactly?
answer: A sink deciding row by row only ever finds out there's a problem after it has already tried, and failed, to write one.
A schema registry checks a brand-new version against its own compatibility rule first, before any consumer is ever handed an event built from it.
